overview: Classification is the task of assigning inputs to discrete categories. Fundamentally, classification is about regions in space, not labels. Each classifier learns: 'Which region of input space belongs to which class?'
A classifier does not say what something is — it says which side of a boundary it falls on. Models compute scores that are converted into class decisions.

topics.title: Decision Boundaries
theory: A decision boundary separates regions of different class predictions. Every classifier = a boundary + a rule.
Boundary types: Linear (line/hyperplane), Non-linear (curves, regions), Piecewise (trees). The choice of classifier determines boundary shape.
visualIntuition: 2D feature space with points colored by class. Boundary drawn as contour, background shaded by predicted class. Animation shows boundary morphing as parameters change.
visualSuggestions: Interactive boundary visualization with parameter controls
Comparison of different classifier boundaries on same data

code.content:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=300,
    n_features=2,
    n_redundant=0,
    n_informative=2,
    n_clusters_per_class=1,
    random_state=42
)

topics.title: Logistic Regression
theory: Despite the name, logistic regression is a linear classifier, not a regression model. Process: Linear combination z = w^T x + b, sigmoid squashes z into probability, threshold → class label.
Sigmoid: σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^(-z)). Maps any real number to (0, 1). Assumes classes are linearly separable and log-odds are linear in features.
Softmax generalizes logistic regression to multiple classes. Classes compete — increasing one probability lowers others. P(y=k) = e^(z_k) / Σ e^(z_j).
visualIntuition: Linear decision boundary with probability gradient (0→1). Sigmoid curve shown separately. Threshold slider shows how predictions change.
visualSuggestions: Probability heatmap overlay on scatter plot
Threshold tuning visualization with false positive/negative counts

code.content:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

model = LogisticRegression()
model.fit(X, y)

y_pred = model.predict(X)
y_prob = model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]

print("Predictions:", y_pred[:5])
print("Probabilities:", y_prob[:5])

topics.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
theory: Cross-entropy measures confidence-weighted error. If model is confident and wrong → large penalty. If unsure → smaller penalty.
Binary cross-entropy: L = -[y·log(p) + (1-y)·log(1-p)]. Wrong confident predictions spike loss dramatically. This is why models learn to be calibrated.
visualIntuition: Loss curve vs probability showing spike near 0 or 1 when prediction is wrong.
visualSuggestions: Interactive loss visualization with draggable prediction probability

code.content:
import numpy as np

def cross_entropy(y_true, y_prob):
    epsilon = 1e-15  # Avoid log(0)
    y_prob = np.clip(y_prob, epsilon, 1 - epsilon)
    return -np.mean(y_true * np.log(y_prob) + (1 - y_true) * np.log(1 - y_prob))

y_true = np.array([1, 0, 1, 1])
y_prob = np.array([0.9, 0.1, 0.8, 0.7])

print("Cross-entropy loss:", cross_entropy(y_true, y_prob))

topics.title: KNN, Naive Bayes, and Decision Trees
theory: KNN classifies by local majority vote. No training — stores data, measures distance. Prediction = most common class among k neighbors. Small k = complex boundary, large k = smooth boundary.
Naive Bayes applies Bayes' Theorem with independence assumption: P(y|x) ∝ P(y)·Π P(x_i|y). 'Naive' because it assumes feature independence — often false but still works well for text.
Decision Trees ask yes/no questions, partition space into rectangles, predict majority class. Easy to interpret but prone to overfitting when grown deep.
visualIntuition: KNN: query point highlighted, k nearest neighbors glow, vote counts shown. Decision tree: feature space splits visualized as rectangles.
visualSuggestions: Interactive k slider showing boundary smoothing

code.description: KNN, Naive Bayes, Decision Tree classifiers
code.content:
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

# KNN
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)
knn.fit(X, y)

# Naive Bayes
nb = GaussianNB()
nb.fit(X, y)

# Decision Tree
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3)
tree.fit(X, y)

print("KNN accuracy:", knn.score(X, y))
print("Naive Bayes accuracy:", nb.score(X, y))
print("Tree accuracy:", tree.score(X, y))

topics.title: Ensemble Classifiers
theory: Random Forest: Many trees with bootstrapped data and random feature subsets. Prediction = majority vote. Reduces variance while maintaining low bias.
Gradient Boosting: Learns sequentially, each model corrects previous errors. Focuses on hard samples. High accuracy but can overfit.
SVM (Support Vector Machine) finds the maximum-margin boundary — the safest boundary is farthest from all points. Kernel trick allows non-linear boundaries without explicit feature expansion.
visualIntuition: Random Forest: individual trees disagree, final decision stabilizes. SVM: margin bands with support vectors highlighted.
visualSuggestions: SVM margin and support vector highlight

code.content:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC

# Random Forest
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100)
rf.fit(X, y)

# Gradient Boosting
gb = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1)
gb.fit(X, y)

# SVM with RBF kernel
svm = SVC(kernel='rbf', gamma=0.5)
svm.fit(X, y)

print("Random Forest accuracy:", rf.score(X, y))
print("Gradient Boosting accuracy:", gb.score(X, y))
print("SVM accuracy:", svm.score(X, y))

topics.title: Imbalanced Datasets and Threshold Tuning
theory: Accuracy fails when classes are imbalanced. Important metrics: Precision (positive predictive value), Recall (sensitivity), F1 (harmonic mean), ROC-AUC.
Classification ≠ fixed threshold. Threshold controls precision vs recall trade-off and business decisions. Moving threshold changes false positive/negative rates.
Strategies for imbalance: resampling (over/undersampling), class weights, SMOTE, focal loss. Choose based on problem and cost of errors.
visualIntuition: Class distribution bars, confusion matrix heatmap. ROC and PR curves with moving threshold marker.
visualSuggestions: Interactive threshold slider with confusion matrix update
ROC vs PR curve comparison for imbalanced data

code.description: Handling imbalanced data and threshold tuning
code.content:
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, roc_curve, precision_recall_curve
import numpy as np

# Get probabilities
y_prob = rf.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]

# Custom threshold
threshold = 0.3
y_custom = (y_prob > threshold).astype(int)

print(classification_report(y, y_custom))

# ROC curve points
fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y, y_prob)
print(f"TPR at threshold 0.5: {tpr[np.argmin(np.abs(thresholds - 0.5))]}")
